faq.a: Prolonged compression can cause irreversible nerve death, leading to permanent paralysis and loss of bladder/bowel control.
Rarely, if the needle damages multiple roots or introduces infection; always use aseptic technique.
faq.q: Can a lumbar puncture cause CES?

faq.a: CES includes saddle anaesthesia and autonomic dysfunction, whereas sciatica has isolated leg pain without bladder/bowel signs.
faq.q: What distinguishes CES from a simple sciatica?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden perineal numbness and inability to void – what is your immediate management? — Recognise CES, order urgent MRI/CT, start bladder catheterisation, arrange neurosurgical decompression.

How does the anatomical position of the cauda equina explain why a central disc herniation at L4‑L5 can cause bilateral leg weakness? — Roots lie together in the canal; central protrusion compresses multiple roots simultaneously.
What bedside test differentiates cauda equina syndrome from a peripheral neuropathy? — Perianal sensation and anal tone; loss points to CES.
Why might a patient with spinal TB develop CES even without a disc herniation? — Granulomatous epidural abscess compresses the roots; consider HIV co‑infection.

Explain why a patient with a high lumbar puncture (L2) is less likely to develop CES than one at L4. — Above L2 the spinal cord is still present; injury affects cord rather than roots, producing different deficits.

In a low‑resource setting without MRI, what imaging strategy can still identify cauda equina compression? — Perform CT myelogram after contrast injection; look for root displacement or epidural collection.

What pharmacologic agents are contraindicated in acute CES before surgery and why? — NSAIDs with anticoagulant effect (e.g., aspirin) increase bleeding risk during decompression; avoid high‑dose steroids unless indicated for edema.
How does the filum terminale differ from the cauda equina roots? — It is a non‑myelinated fibrous strand that anchors the cord, lacking sensory or motor fibers.
ai.title: Cauda Equina Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The cauda equina is the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots that descend below the conus medullaris. Understanding its location, relations, and blood supply helps recognise cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency common in low‑resource settings.

b: Forms the peripheral component of the lumbosacral plexus
Contains motor, sensory and autonomic fibers
sections.p: The cauda equina (Latin “horse’s tail”) consists of the L2‑S5 spinal nerve roots and the filum terminale that continue within the lumbar cistern after the spinal cord ends at L1‑L2.

b: Roots spread like a horse’s tail
Each root is surrounded by CSF, allowing easy displacement
sections.p: It lies in the subarachnoid space of the vertebral canal, filling the lumbar enlargement of the dural sac from the lower border of L1 to the sacral hiatus.

b: Close to lumbar vertebral bodies – disc herniation is a common cause of compression
Adjacent to the internal vertebral venous plexus
sections.p: Anteriorly the cauda equina rests on the posterior longitudinal ligament and intervertebral discs; posteriorly it is covered by the dura mater and epidural fat.

b: Vasa nervorum provide oxygen to each root
Ischemia can worsen compression injuries
sections.p: Arterial supply derives from the lumbar segmental arteries (branches of the aorta) and the sacral arteries, forming a rich anastomotic network around the roots.

b: S2‑S4 roots form the pudendal nerve (perineal sensation, sphincter control)
L2‑L4 roots contribute to the femoral and obturator nerves
sections.p: Motor fibers exit to innervate the lower limb muscles; sensory fibers convey cutaneous sensation from the perineum (saddle area) and lower extremities; autonomic fibers control bladder, bowel and sexual function.

b: Allows voluntary foot movement
Enables bladder emptying and anal continence
sections.p: Collectively the roots provide motor control of the lower limbs, sensory input from the legs and perineum, and parasympathetic outflow to pelvic viscera.

b: Large central disc herniation (most common in low‑resource hospitals)
Spinal epidural abscess (TB, bacterial, fungal – consider HIV, malaria co‑infection)
Post‑traumatic fracture‑dislocation
Tumours (e.g., schwannoma, metastasis)
Iatrogenic injury during lumbar puncture
sections.p: Compression or trauma to the cauda equina produces cauda equina syndrome (CES), a surgical emergency characterised by saddle anaesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction and LMN leg weakness.

b: Test perianal sensation with a cotton wisp – loss suggests S2‑S4 involvement
Assess anal tone by digital rectal exam – reduced tone indicates CES
Bulbocavernosus reflex: tap the glans penis/clitoris, observe anal sphincter contraction
sections.p: Key bedside tests focus on motor, sensory and autonomic function of the lumbosacral roots.

t.b: Shows compression of nerve roots; if unavailable, CT myelogram can be used
Identifies fractures or severe disc space collapse when advanced imaging is lacking

whenToSeekHelp: Acute urinary retention or overflow incontinence
